TL;DR, The following is a pretty long post that rambles on a couple different topics, but the answer to your specific question is in the next 2 or 3 paragaphs. The rest is me speculating.

First, I know it is legal to design a cam to pull the trigger by turning a crank. That is still considered semi-auto and as long as you don't do anything else to change its characteristics you are okay. For instance if you wanted to put it on a semiauto shotgun you'd still be restricted in how short the barrel could be.

Second, I also know the ATF has cleared the Fostech system because although it can shoot twice with one trigger pull, the second shot is only fired by releasing the trigger and it must be pulled again to fire again.

I do not know their views on putting a cam in a rifle with a Fostech system. I also do not know their views if you have one crank with two cams, essentially firing two rifles that are joined together. Theoretically, I would think the legal analysis should reach the same result. They seem to take the language very literally, so as long as the trigger needs to be pulled for each shot, it doesn't seem to matter how quickly that can be done or if there is another mechansm between your fingers and the trigger.

That said, I am definitely not making something like that much less selling it to someone without getting all my ducks in row. I don't look good in orange and I hate institutional food. I'm pretty sure an actual gatling gun is Title 2, but I'm not sure why. It isn't really a machine gun (at least based on the definition as I understand it), so I suspect it is captured by a different definition entirely or there is some other factor in the definition of machine gun I don't yet know.

DependIng on design, I could even see the kit qualifying as firearm itself and requiring the proper markings, serial number & manufacturer's name (which is another thing they are extremely precise about).

I will definitely need to find that out if I go forward, but I was planning on getting a license anyway, so I was already going to talk to them. I also met one of their lawyers a couple months ago. Though I don't really practice law anymore (and haven't for a while), I keep my license active just in case and that involves getting a certain number of continuing legal education (CLE) hours every year. Anyway this guy from the ATF was teaching a portion of a CLE course focusing on gun laws. Unfortunately the course didn't really cover any of these issues (apart from manufactured guns needing proper markings). He seemed like a pretty nice, helpful guy, and I have his office direct dial phone number and his work email so I may reach out to him informally to make sure he agrees with my approach to asking them for a ruling.

Having dealt with a lot of Federal regulators and/or agencies (including IRS, SEC, NOAA, FCC, FBI, OFAC) I have found you can never talk to them too early or too often. (Though sometimes you may want to make your early calls on a no name basis, especially if you are looking into self-reporting some type of violation.)

If anyone is interested, that course was mostly focused on estate planning for people with large collections (especially if they have Title 2 guns). How move them around, transfer them either as "gifts" or as inheritances, allow groups of people from different states to share ownership through trusts, etc. It was very interesting. I can't legitimately copy the materials, but if anyone has questions, I could pull them out and try to summarize answers.
